records.text: Erika Kirk was effectively placing a long Us Weekly advertisement attacking Candace Owens and calling her demonic.
records.speaker: Candace Owens

appearances.snippet: Us Weekly sends me an email yesterday that's like. four pages long telling me i have 24 hours to respond they're already publishing it in print and it's basically just an ad uh it's basically Erika (Erika Kirk) is putting in an ad in us weekly that's what she's doing um and it's just going to be one long article attacking me and calling me demonic um uh and quoting her friends tracy martin they've obviously been working on this for weeks tracy martin James Kaddis who runs the faith department the most despicable department at turning point usa

verification.notes: The phrase effectively placing an advertisement is an interpretation of editorial motive. Searches found the feud and an upcoming Us Weekly inquiry but no contract, payment, commissioning record, or independent evidence that Erika Kirk placed an advertisement or controlled the article.

records.text: Us Weekly gave Candace Owens 24 hours to respond to an Erika Kirk story that was already being printed.
records.speaker: Candace Owens

appearances.snippet: It's going to be published in the next issue on Thursday, June 11th. It's June 10th. I got this email last night. You can see it's 6.10 p.m. And we'll be on stands on June 17th. So they're already printing this and we're just telling you here's what we've heard.

verification.notes: The transcript displays and reads an alleged inquiry email with a next-day deadline and later newsstand date. Searches located Owens reposting the claim but no authenticated email headers, Us Weekly confirmation, or independent recipient record sufficient to verify the exact 24-hour notice and print status.

records.text: The Us Weekly hit piece was written under a fake byline used as a sock-puppet account rather than by a real journalist.
records.speaker: Candace Owens

appearances.snippet: uh charlie and i almost exclusively texted and so it's just it just it's just a hit piece written by a person who doesn't actually exist so what they do when they don't want to put their name behind something they have these like they're like sock puppet accounts so it's like a fake name like paula leva um and they're not real people but they keep publishing under these people as if they are real people i don't know if you guys know what this is how this happens in the media where there's literally non-existent journalists um and this is one of those pieces so this is how turning point operates

verification.notes: Prior reporting established that a contractor used fake AI bylines for some Us Weekly commerce content. Searches found no evidence tying the specific Erika Kirk story or its named byline to that contractor, a sock-puppet identity, or a nonexistent journalist.
